title: AI Engineering Atlas
subtitle: A field guide from a promising idea to a useful system.
description: Follow one help-center assistant through five practical chapters: define the task, ground answers in evidence, design the workflow, evaluate behavior, and operate with care.

chapters.title: Frame the problem
chapters.summary: Turn a promising AI use case into a task you can test.

sections.heading: Choose a task
sections.text: The support team wants to reduce time spent on repeat questions. Start with one job: answer public help-center questions using approved articles. Account-specific requests and topics with conflicting evidence go to a human.

sections.heading: Measure the current workflow
sections.text: Sample real cases with personal details removed. Time a support teammate using ordinary search, then record whether the answer is correct and supported. Keep the same cases for the model comparison.

sections.heading: Write a release test
sections.text: Agree on an acceptable success rate, the maximum latency, and which mistakes require escalation. Hold back cases for release evaluation and inspect results by request type before expanding access.

chapters.callout: For the help-center assistant, a confident answer about the wrong refund policy can be more costly than handing the case to a human.

quiz.prompt: What is the first task in the running example?
quiz.correct: Answer public help-center questions from approved articles
quiz.distractor: Handle every request the support team receives
quiz.rationale: A narrow task makes the audience, input, and acceptable output clear.

quiz.prompt: What should you compare the assistant against?
quiz.correct: The current human and search workflow
quiz.distractor: An unrelated chatbot demo
quiz.rationale: The baseline shows what users already get on the same kind of task.

quiz.prompt: Which question belongs in the release set?
quiz.correct: A realistic question with conflicting policy evidence
quiz.distractor: A question copied into every prompt example
quiz.rationale: Conflicting evidence tests a behavior that matters and should stay unseen during tuning.

quiz.prompt: Which measure best checks a supported answer?
quiz.correct: The answer is correct and its cited passage supports the claim
quiz.distractor: The answer includes a link of any kind
quiz.rationale: A citation only helps if it supports what the assistant said.

quiz.prompt: What should happen with an account-specific request?
quiz.correct: Send it to the appropriate human support path
quiz.distractor: Assume the most common account configuration
quiz.rationale: Account-specific cases fall outside the public help-center task.

quiz.prompt: When should the team agree on release thresholds?
quiz.correct: Before reviewing release scores
quiz.distractor: After seeing which results look strongest
quiz.rationale: Earlier agreement prevents the test from shifting to fit the results.

quiz.prompt: Which dataset best supports a fair comparison?
quiz.correct: The same representative cases for both workflows
quiz.distractor: Easy cases for the assistant and hard cases for the baseline
quiz.rationale: Shared cases make the comparison interpretable.

quiz.prompt: How should sampled support cases be prepared?
quiz.correct: Remove personal details while preserving the task
quiz.distractor: Keep all identifying details by default
quiz.rationale: The evaluation needs the scenario, not the identity of the person who raised it.

quiz.prompt: Which best describes an operational constraint?
quiz.correct: The service should respond within an agreed time budget
quiz.distractor: The product should feel impressive
quiz.rationale: A time budget can be measured and tied to the user experience.

quiz.prompt: Which is an example of a high-impact mistake?
quiz.correct: A confident answer using the wrong refund policy
quiz.distractor: A truthful response that offers escalation
quiz.rationale: The incorrect policy can mislead the user into making a consequential decision.

quiz.prompt: Why retain a holdout set?
quiz.correct: To assess how the system handles cases it was not tuned on
quiz.distractor: To make those questions available as prompt examples
quiz.rationale: A holdout measures behavior on cases unseen during iteration.

quiz.prompt: What can the baseline reveal before building an assistant?
quiz.correct: That ordinary search already meets the target
quiz.distractor: That a model is necessary for every case
quiz.rationale: Measuring existing performance can change whether a proposed feature is worth building.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in a useful task specification?
quiz.correct: The intended user, task, success criteria, and escalation policy
quiz.distractor: A model name with a broad mission statement
quiz.rationale: A specification explains who the feature serves and how its behavior will be judged.

quiz.prompt: Which result warrants a closer look?
quiz.correct: Strong overall results with poor performance on refunds
quiz.distractor: An improvement across all measured categories
quiz.rationale: A high-impact category may matter more than its share of the average.

quiz.prompt: What should happen when approved sources disagree?
quiz.correct: Escalate rather than invent a definitive answer
quiz.distractor: Always choose the shorter article
quiz.rationale: The running example treats conflicting evidence as a reason for human review.

quiz.prompt: How can the team grade speed fairly?
quiz.correct: Measure comparable tasks from the same starting point
quiz.distractor: Compare model generation alone to the whole support interaction
quiz.rationale: Comparable boundaries make timing measurements useful.

quiz.prompt: Who can help identify acceptable failure behavior?
quiz.correct: The people who own and handle escalated support cases
quiz.distractor: Only the person who wrote the prompt
quiz.rationale: Support owners know where errors cause extra work or harm.

quiz.prompt: Which is the clearest next step after a release-blocking result?
quiz.correct: Investigate the failure and rerun the release test after a fix
quiz.distractor: Remove that class of case from the test
quiz.rationale: The result is evidence that the tested version misses an agreed threshold.

quiz.prompt: What is a legitimate product outcome for an unsupported question?
quiz.correct: A clear handoff to the next available support channel
quiz.distractor: A fluent guess to keep the answer rate high
quiz.rationale: A handoff preserves usefulness when the system lacks evidence.

quiz.prompt: When should the team consider broadening the scope?
quiz.correct: After the current task meets its criteria and the new task has its own test plan
quiz.distractor: As soon as the first example works in a demo
quiz.rationale: Broader scope introduces different cases and failure costs.

chapters.title: Ground the system
chapters.summary: Give the system useful evidence and make its answers traceable.

sections.heading: Organize sources
sections.text: Use approved help-center articles and revision dates. Preserve headings and links when preparing text for search.

sections.heading: Test retrieval
sections.text: Look at what search actually finds for common, ambiguous, and outdated questions before testing the final answer.

sections.heading: Make evidence visible
sections.text: Return source links so readers can check the claim. Route questions with missing or conflicting material for review.

chapters.callout: A link is useful when the linked passage supports the actual claim.

quiz.prompt: What should retrieval first be tested against?
quiz.correct: Questions whose needed sources are known
quiz.distractor: Only the first article in the index
quiz.rationale: Known source targets help diagnose retrieval separately from generation.

quiz.prompt: What makes a citation useful?
quiz.correct: Its passage supports the claim
quiz.distractor: The article is long
quiz.rationale: A reader needs a source that verifies the particular claim.

chapters.title: Design the workflow
chapters.summary: Decide where a model, a fixed step, or a human belongs.

sections.heading: Draw the workflow
sections.text: Separate question triage, retrieval, drafting, and publication. Give each step a clear input and output.

sections.heading: Choose where to use a model
sections.text: A model can propose an answer from text. A fixed check can make sure source IDs came back with the evidence.

sections.heading: Define the handoff
sections.text: When a case needs a person, send the original question, relevant evidence, and the reason for escalation.

chapters.callout: Give the next person enough context to pick up the case without repeating the whole workflow.

quiz.prompt: Which job suits a fixed check?
quiz.correct: Check that every cited ID came from retrieval
quiz.distractor: Write a nuanced natural-language summary
quiz.rationale: ID membership can be checked directly.

quiz.prompt: What should an escalation include?
quiz.correct: The question, evidence, and reason for handoff
quiz.distractor: A generic notification
quiz.rationale: The added context lets the next person continue the work.

chapters.title: Evaluate behavior
chapters.summary: Build an evaluation set that reveals how changes affect actual cases.

sections.heading: Cover important cases
sections.text: Sample routine questions, conflicting policies, unanswered questions, and requests that require a human.

sections.heading: Grade separate behaviors
sections.text: Track correctness, evidence use, and appropriate escalation as distinct judgments. Keep examples that show where reviewers differ.

sections.heading: Inspect changes by category
sections.text: Compare results against the earlier release and read representative failures before drawing conclusions.

chapters.callout: An overall improvement can hide a regression in a small but high-impact category.

quiz.prompt: What can a single overall score miss?
quiz.correct: A regression in a small category
quiz.distractor: Every improvement in a large category
quiz.rationale: Separate numbers reveal how changes affect smaller groups.

quiz.prompt: What should you retain alongside aggregate results?
quiz.correct: Case-level examples and judgments
quiz.distractor: Only the final percentage
quiz.rationale: Examples support investigation and useful reviewer disagreement.

chapters.title: Operate in production
chapters.summary: Set a service target and give operators a way to recover.

sections.heading: Decide what to monitor
sections.text: Track response time, answer rate, escalation volume, and whether cited sources still exist.

sections.heading: Prepare recovery
sections.text: Document how to disable generated answers and restore the previous published version. Include ownership and the conditions that trigger that switch.

sections.heading: Review changes in stages
sections.text: Start with a small share of cases. Compare new outcomes to the release thresholds before expanding.

chapters.callout: Practice turning off generated answers while the ordinary help-center search stays available.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in the recovery plan?
quiz.correct: How to disable generated answers and who owns the action
quiz.distractor: A promise to investigate after any incident
quiz.rationale: Operators need a specific action and clear ownership.

quiz.prompt: How should a new release first reach users?
quiz.correct: Serve a small share of cases and review the result
quiz.distractor: Replace the previous version for everyone immediately
quiz.rationale: A staged rollout makes it easier to contain and inspect unexpected outcomes.
